I'm pretty sure this question violates causality. But since that's not against the rules (thank god you had a question mark) I guess it depends on how serious you'd like to get. If you're remotely serious, you'll want a DSLR probably and they're not cheap. A Canon Rebel is probably enough to get you started and teach you the basics but you'll eventually want to move on to something better if you keep at it.

Someone else suggested taking photos and of course that's the most important thing, but apart from that, I would study photos that you like and try to deconstruct the elements you like about them. Not to directly copy them but to incorporate certain aspects into your own work when it makes sense. Maybe there's something about the focal length, the framing, the angle of a light. Figure out why you like that picture over other pictures of the same kind of thing and tuck that difference away in your memory. And keep shooting.

https://www.voat.co/v/photography/

TONS of online resources available to help you understand the mechanics of a camera and the basics.

But really, just keep taking pictures. Eventually you figure out what to look for, and how to frame it and how to adjust your camera to capture what you had in mind.

And for god sake, don't chimp. You are more likely to miss a moment if you snap a pic and immediately look at it and "Ooohhh Ahhhhh" (ergo "chimping").

The same way you become a writer: start doing it. The most important things in photography are lighting and framing, neither if which has anything to do with the camera. I can get some pretty damn good shots with my cell phone camera just by paying attention to lighting and how things are framed. Once you get a handle on that, then you'll want to start playing with exposure times, focal distances, and the like. That's when you need a proper camera body. I strongly recommend going either Canon or Nikon, as those are the most popular in the industry. However, once you pick, you're gonna be married to it: the lenses don't interchange, and you can sink a LOT of money into glass. Figure a low f-stop telephoto is in the $3k range, if not more.
